title: HIS 122 Exam 2: Chapters 27-30

concepts.name: Ch 27: Ottomans, Safavids, Mughals
concepts.gist: The three Islamic gunpowder empires and their rulers.

concepts.name: Ch 28: Revolutions and nationalism
concepts.gist: Enlightenment ideas, the Atlantic revolutions, and the new nation-states.

concepts.name: Ch 29: Industrial Revolution
concepts.gist: Machines, factories, and the ideas that answered them.

concepts.name: Ch 30: The Americas
concepts.gist: US expansion, the Civil War, and the Mexican Revolution.

notes.Ottoman Empire: Turkish Sunni empire, about 1300 to 1922, that ruled the Middle East, North Africa and southeastern Europe from Constantinople.
notes.Janissaries: The sultan's elite infantry: Christian boys taken through the devshirme, converted to Islam and trained as soldiers.
notes.Mehmed II: "The Conqueror." Took Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire.
notes.Suleyman the Magnificent: Ruled 1520-66 at the Ottoman peak. Called "the Lawgiver"; pushed into Hungary and besieged Vienna in 1529.
notes.Safavid Empire: Persian empire, 1501-1736, that made Shia Islam the state religion. Rival of the Sunni Ottomans.
notes.Shah Abbas the Great: Greatest Safavid shah, 1588-1629. Reformed the army, built up Isfahan and encouraged trade.
notes.Mughal Empire: Muslim dynasty, founded by Babur in 1526, that ruled most of India.
notes.Akbar: Mughal emperor, 1556-1605, known for religious tolerance: ended the tax on non-Muslims and brought Hindus into government.
notes.Aurangzeb: Mughal emperor, 1658-1707. Pushed the empire to its largest size but ended Akbar's tolerance, which fueled revolts.
notes.Taj Mahal: White marble tomb at Agra, built by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
notes.The Enlightenment: 1700s movement that applied reason to society and government: natural rights, consent of the governed, limits on power.
notes.John Locke: English thinker: people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and may replace a government that violates them.
notes.Popular sovereignty: The idea that a government's authority comes from the people, not from God or a king.
notes.American Revolution: 1775-83. Thirteen British colonies won independence after disputes over taxes and representation.
notes.Declaration of Independence: 1776. Jefferson's statement of natural rights and of the colonies' break from Britain.
notes.George Washington: Commander of the Continental Army, then the first US president.
notes.French Revolution: Began in 1789. Overthrew the monarchy and the old social order in the name of liberty, equality and fraternity.
notes.Louis XVI: King of France when the revolution began. Executed by guillotine in 1793.
notes.Estates General: France's assembly of clergy, nobles and commoners, called in 1789 for the first time since 1614. The Third Estate broke away as the National Assembly.
notes.Maximilien Robespierre: Jacobin leader of the Committee of Public Safety. Ran the Terror until he was guillotined in 1794.
notes.Reign of Terror: 1793-94. The revolutionary government executed thousands of suspected enemies.
notes.Napoleon Bonaparte: General who seized power in 1799, crowned himself emperor in 1804, conquered much of Europe and fell at Waterloo in 1815.
notes.Haitian Revolution: 1791-1804. Enslaved people in French Saint-Domingue won freedom and independence, led at first by Toussaint Louverture.
notes.Simon Bolivar: "The Liberator." Led the independence wars against Spain across northern South America.
notes.William Wilberforce: British member of Parliament who led the campaign that abolished Britain's slave trade in 1807.
notes.Elizabeth Cady Stanton: US women's rights leader. Organized the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848.
notes.Nationalism: Loyalty to a nation of shared language, culture and history. It drove the unifications of Italy and Germany.
notes.Zionism: Movement for a Jewish national homeland in Palestine, organized by Theodor Herzl in the 1890s.
notes.Congress of Vienna: 1814-15 meeting, led by Austria's Metternich, that restored monarchies and a balance of power after Napoleon.
notes.Giuseppe Garibaldi: Nationalist whose volunteer Red Shirts conquered southern Italy in 1860, helping unify the country.
notes.Otto von Bismarck: Prussian chancellor who unified Germany in 1871 through "blood and iron."
notes.Industrial Revolution: The shift from hand work to machine production, starting in Britain around 1750 with textiles, coal and steam.
notes.James Watt: Scottish engineer whose improved steam engine of 1769 made steam power practical for factories.
notes.The factory system: Workers and machines gathered in one place under set hours and a division of labor, replacing work at home.
notes.Luddites: English textile workers who smashed machines in the 1810s to protest lost jobs and wages.
notes.Eli Whitney: Invented the cotton gin in 1793, which expanded slavery, and promoted interchangeable parts.
notes.Henry Ford: Used the moving assembly line, from 1913, to mass-produce the affordable Model T.
notes.Socialism: The idea that society, not private owners, should own or control the means of production.
notes.Karl Marx: Co-wrote the Communist Manifesto in 1848: history is class struggle, and workers will overthrow capitalism.
notes.Proletariat: Marx's term for the industrial working class, who own only their labor. Their opposite is the bourgeoisie.
notes.Manifest Destiny: 1840s belief that the United States was destined to spread across North America.
notes.Indian Removal Act: 1830 law, signed by Andrew Jackson, forcing Native nations in the Southeast to move west of the Mississippi.
notes.Trail of Tears: The forced march of the Cherokee to Indian Territory in 1838-39. Thousands died.
notes.Little Bighorn: 1876. Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors wiped out Custer's 7th Cavalry in Montana.
notes.Abraham Lincoln: President during the Civil War. Issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863; assassinated in 1865.
notes.The Civil War: 1861-65. Eleven Southern states seceded over slavery. The Union's victory ended slavery and kept the country together.
notes.Mexican Revolution: 1910-20. Overthrew Porfirio Diaz. Zapata and Villa fought for land reform, and it produced the 1917 constitution.

test.q: The devshirme supplied the Ottoman state with what?
options: Christian boys trained as Janissaries and officials
Tax revenue from the silk trade
test.why: The levy took boys from Christian villages. The best became soldiers and administrators loyal only to the sultan.

test.q: Which technology was decisive in the fall of Constantinople in 1453?
test.why: Ottoman bombards battered walls that had held for a thousand years. Greek fire was a Byzantine weapon.

test.q: Suleyman is called "Kanuni" in Turkish. What does the title refer to?
options: His reform of the empire's laws
test.why: Kanuni means lawgiver. He never took Vienna: the 1529 siege failed.

test.q: Why did the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514 matter?
options: It halted Safavid expansion west and hardened the Sunni-Shia frontier with the Ottomans
It gave the Safavids control of Constantinople
test.why: Ottoman guns beat Safavid cavalry, fixing a border and a religious divide between the two empires.

test.q: Shah Abbas strengthened the Safavid state in all of these ways EXCEPT:
options: Making Sunni Islam the state religion
Building a standing army with firearms
test.why: The Safavids stayed firmly Shia. The other three are his reforms.

test.q: Which policy most separates Aurangzeb from Akbar?
options: He brought back the jizya and enforced Islamic law more strictly
He gave Hindus more high offices
He abandoned Islam for a new faith
test.why: Akbar had ended the tax on non-Muslims. Aurangzeb restored it, which fueled revolts.

test.q: Who overthrew and imprisoned the builder of the Taj Mahal?
test.why: Aurangzeb deposed Shah Jahan in 1658 and held him in Agra Fort.

test.q: Which statement about the three "gunpowder empires" is accurate?
options: The Mughals were Muslim rulers of a mostly Hindu population
The Safavids were Sunni and the Ottomans Shia
The Ottomans were centered in Persia
test.why: Ottomans: Sunni, based in Anatolia. Safavids: Shia, in Persia. Mughals: a Muslim dynasty over Hindu-majority India.

test.q: Separation of powers is most closely tied to which thinker?
test.why: Montesquieu argued for dividing power among branches of government.

test.q: Which Enlightenment idea appears most directly in the Declaration of Independence?
options: Natural rights and government by consent
test.why: Jefferson adapted Locke: unalienable rights, and governments that draw their power from the consent of the governed.

test.q: What did the Third Estate create when it broke away from the Estates General?
test.why: Denied a vote per person, the commoners declared themselves the National Assembly in June 1789.

test.q: Which pairing of a person and their part in the French Revolution is correct?
options: Robespierre: led the Committee of Public Safety during the Terror
Louis XVI: led the storming of the Bastille
test.why: Louis XVI called the Estates General and was executed. Robespierre ran the Terror. Napoleon seized power in 1799 and later crowned himself emperor.

test.q: Who brought Robespierre down?
options: Members of his own National Convention
test.why: Fearing they were next, deputies had him arrested in July 1794.

test.q: France's defeat in Saint-Domingue led Napoleon to do what?
options: Sell Louisiana to the United States
Free every enslaved person in France's colonies
test.why: Without Haiti, a North American empire made no sense. He sold Louisiana in 1803.

test.q: Bolivar's independence movement was led mainly by which group?
options: Creoles: American-born people of Spanish descent
test.why: Creoles resented being shut out of top posts by officials sent from Spain.

test.q: Metternich's aims at Vienna included all of these EXCEPT:
test.why: Metternich saw nationalism and liberalism as threats to the old order.

test.q: What best contrasts Garibaldi and Bismarck?
options: Garibaldi led volunteers from below; Bismarck used state power and war from above
Garibaldi was a king; Bismarck was a rebel
Garibaldi unified Germany; Bismarck unified Italy
test.why: Italy's south was won by a volunteer army. Germany was built by Prussia's government and its wars.

test.q: Which event convinced Theodor Herzl that Jews needed a state of their own?
test.why: A Jewish French officer was falsely convicted of treason amid open antisemitism.

test.q: What did Britain's act of 1807 actually do?
options: Ended the British slave trade, but not slavery itself
Freed all enslaved people in the empire
Ended slavery in the United States
test.why: Slavery in the empire was abolished later, in 1833.

test.q: The Declaration of Sentiments was modeled on which document?
test.why: It opens by adding two words: "all men and women are created equal."

test.q: Nationalism was most dangerous to which kind of state?
options: Empires of many peoples, like Austria and the Ottomans
test.why: If every people deserves its own nation, an empire of many peoples comes apart.

test.q: Which of Napoleon's actions did most to spread the Revolution's ideas across Europe?
options: Imposing the Napoleonic Code in the lands he conquered
test.why: The code carried legal equality and the end of feudal privilege along with his armies.

test.q: Which precedent did Washington set at the end of his presidency?
test.why: He stepped down in 1797, and presidents followed that example for almost 150 years.

test.q: Popular sovereignty is the direct opposite of which idea?
test.why: One says authority comes up from the people, the other that it comes down from God.

test.q: According to Locke, what may people do if a government violates their natural rights?
options: Nothing: rulers answer only to God
test.why: Government is a contract. Break it, and the people may form a new one.

test.q: Britain industrialized first for all of these reasons EXCEPT:
options: A large population of serfs bound to the land
test.why: Britain had no serfdom. Its workers were free to move to factory towns.

test.q: What was Watt's key improvement to the steam engine?
test.why: Condensing the steam in a separate chamber stopped the cylinder from being reheated on every stroke.

test.q: What did the Luddites mainly object to?
options: Machines that let employers replace skilled workers with cheaper labor
The end of the slave trade
test.why: They were skilled workers defending their trades and wages, not people afraid of technology.

test.q: Besides the cotton gin, Eli Whitney is known for promoting what?
test.why: He championed identical parts for muskets, a step toward mass production.

test.q: Which of these was NOT part of Ford's system?
options: Craftsmen building one whole car at a time
Each worker repeating a single task
Higher wages, such as the five-dollar day
test.why: Ford replaced craft building with a line of simple, repeated tasks.

test.q: According to Marx, what drives history?
test.why: The Communist Manifesto opens with it: all history is the history of class struggles.

test.q: How did Robert Owen differ from Karl Marx?
options: He tried to build cooperative model communities instead of calling for revolution
He rejected any change to factory life
He wanted workers to seize the state by force
test.why: Owen was a utopian socialist: show a better way and others will copy it. Marx expected revolution.

test.q: In Marx's terms, the bourgeoisie are:
options: The owners of the means of production
test.why: Bourgeoisie own the factories and capital. The proletariat work for wages.

test.q: Which change defined the factory system?
options: Workers gathered in one place under set hours and close supervision
Families spinning at home at their own pace
test.why: It replaced the domestic system, where work was done at home.

test.q: Manifest Destiny led most directly to which conflict?
test.why: Expansion into Texas and the Southwest brought war, and Mexico lost about half its territory.

test.q: Which branch of the US government sided with the Cherokee before removal?
test.why: The Court ruled for the Cherokee in 1832. President Jackson refused to enforce the ruling.

test.q: Who signed the treaty the US used to justify the Trail of Tears?
options: A small Cherokee faction, without the nation's consent
The Cherokee principal chief, John Ross
test.why: The 1835 treaty was signed by a minority. Ross and most Cherokee rejected it.

test.q: What was the longer-term result of Little Bighorn?
options: The US Army stepped up its campaign and Plains resistance collapsed within a few years
The Army left the northern Plains
test.why: The victory shocked the country, and the government answered with overwhelming force.

test.q: Which advantage most helped the Union win?
options: Better generals at the start of the war
test.why: The North could out-produce and out-supply the South in a long war.

test.q: Why did the Emancipation Proclamation not free enslaved people in Kentucky or Maryland?
options: It applied only to areas in rebellion, and those states stayed in the Union
The Supreme Court struck it down
test.why: It was a war measure against the Confederacy. The 13th Amendment ended slavery everywhere.

test.q: What was Emiliano Zapata's central demand?
test.why: His slogan was "land and liberty."

anchors: Defeat at the gates of Vienna

what.head: Six centuries of empire
lines: Starts as a small Turkish state in Anatolia.
Takes Constantinople in 1453 and rules on three continents.
Collapses after World War I. Turkey replaces it.

when.label: 1300s–1826
anchors: Sultan Mahmud II destroys the corps

what.head: The sultan's slave soldiers
lines: Christian boys are taken, converted to Islam and trained.
They become the empire's elite infantry, armed with guns.
They grow so powerful that a sultan destroys them in 1826.

what.head: Constantinople falls
lines: Giant cannons break walls that had held for a thousand years.
The Byzantine Empire ends.
The city becomes the Ottoman capital.

where.name: Istanbul
where.today: An empire from Hungary to Iraq

what.head: The Ottoman peak
lines: Conquers Belgrade, Rhodes and most of Hungary.
Besieges Vienna in 1529 but cannot take it.
Rewrites the law code and fills Istanbul with mosques.

who.name: Shah Ismail I
chips: Made Shia Islam the state religion

what.head: A Shia empire in Persia
lines: Ismail unites Persia and makes Shia Islam official.
That sets the Safavids against the Sunni Ottomans next door.
The empire peaks under Shah Abbas, then falls in the 1700s.

who.name: Shah Abbas I
chips: Built a standing army with guns

what.head: Persia's golden age
lines: Builds a standing army with muskets and cannon.
Wins back land from the Ottomans and the Uzbeks.
Makes Isfahan a great city and a hub of the silk trade.

anchors: Aurangzeb dies and decline sets in

who.name: Babur
who.role: Founder, descended from Timur and Genghis Khan

what.head: Muslim rulers of a Hindu-majority land
lines: Babur invades from Central Asia and takes Delhi in 1526.
Akbar builds a rich, tolerant empire.
It weakens after Aurangzeb, and Britain ends it in 1857.

what.head: Rule by tolerance
lines: Ends the jizya, the tax on non-Muslims.
Gives Hindus high office and marries Rajput princesses.
Hosts debates among Muslims, Hindus, Christians and others.

anchors: Taj Mahal begun by his father

what.head: Biggest empire, deepest cracks
lines: Pushes Mughal rule over almost all of India.
Brings back the jizya and enforces strict Islamic law.
Decades of war and revolt drain the empire.

what.head: A tomb built for love
lines: Mumtaz Mahal dies giving birth to their 14th child.
Her white marble tomb takes about twenty years to finish.
Shah Jahan is later buried beside her.

when.label: 1690s–1780s
when.fine: The "Age of Reason", about a century long

where.name: Paris
where.today: Salons of France, then all of Europe

who.name: Voltaire
who.role: French writer who championed free speech and tolerance

what.head: Reason over tradition
lines: Thinkers apply reason to government, religion and society.
Key ideas: natural rights, consent of the governed, separation of powers.
Those ideas fuel the American and French revolutions.

what.head: Government by consent
lines: People are born with rights to life, liberty and property.
Governments exist to protect those rights.
If a government fails, the people may replace it.

anchors: "We the People" opens the US Constitution

what.head: Power comes from the people
lines: Rulers get their authority from the consent of the people.
That rejects the divine right of kings.
It becomes the basis of the US and French constitutions.

what.head: Colonies break from Britain
lines: Colonists protest taxes passed without their consent.
War begins at Lexington and Concord in 1775.
Britain recognizes independence in 1783.

what.head: "All men are created equal"
lines: Congress adopts it on July 4, 1776.
It says people have rights no government can take away.
It lists the king's abuses and declares the colonies free.

what.head: The general who gave up power
lines: Holds the Continental Army together for eight years.
Wins at Yorktown with French help.
Serves two terms as president, then walks away.

what.head: Liberty, equality, fraternity
lines: A bankrupt monarchy calls the Estates General in 1789.
Commoners form the National Assembly, and Paris storms the Bastille.
The king is executed, and it ends with Napoleon in power.

where.name: Versailles
where.today: The royal palace near Paris, France

who.name: Louis XVI
who.role: King of France when the Revolution began

what.head: The king who lost his head
lines: Inherits huge debts and cannot fix them.
Tries to flee France in 1791 and is caught.
Is tried for treason and guillotined in January 1793.

anchors: Its last meeting before this one

where.name: Versailles
where.today: The royal palace near Paris, France

what.head: The meeting that started it
lines: The king summons it to approve new taxes.
The Third Estate demands one vote per person, not per estate.
Refused, it declares itself the National Assembly.

what.head: From idealist to executioner
lines: Speaks for the poor and for a republic of virtue.
Leads the Committee of Public Safety through the Terror.
Is arrested by his own Convention and guillotined.

who.name: The Committee of Public Safety
who.role: Twelve men who ran France in the emergency

what.head: The Terror
lines: France is at war abroad and in revolt at home.
The government hunts "enemies of the Revolution."
It ends when Robespierre himself goes to the guillotine.

who.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
who.role: General, then emperor of the French

what.head: Empire by conquest
lines: Seizes power in a coup in 1799.
Conquers much of Europe and spreads the Napoleonic Code.
Loses in Russia, then at Waterloo, and dies in exile.

who.name: Toussaint Louverture
who.role: Formerly enslaved general who led the revolt

what.head: Enslaved people win a nation
lines: Enslaved workers in France's richest colony rise up.
They defeat Napoleon's army.
1804: Haiti declares independence.

what.head: Freeing a continent
lines: Leads creole armies against Spanish rule.
Frees Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia.
His dream of one united Gran Colombia falls apart.

who.name: William Wilberforce
who.role: Member of Parliament and evangelical reformer

what.head: Ending Britain's slave trade
lines: Brings abolition bills to Parliament year after year.
The Slave Trade Act passes in 1807.
Slavery itself is abolished in the empire in 1833, days before he dies.

anchors: Founds a suffrage group with Susan B. Anthony

what.head: "All men and women are created equal"
lines: Organizes the first women's rights convention in 1848.
Its declaration demands the right to vote.
She dies 18 years before the 19th Amendment.

when.label: 1800s
when.fine: The force that redrew Europe's map

who.name: Giuseppe Mazzini
who.role: Italian nationalist, founder of Young Italy

what.head: One people, one state
lines: People who share a language and a history want their own nation.
It unites Italy and Germany.
It pulls apart empires of many peoples, like Austria and the Ottomans.

where.name: Basel
where.today: Switzerland, site of the first Zionist Congress

who.name: Theodor Herzl
who.role: Journalist from Vienna, founder of political Zionism

what.head: A homeland for the Jewish people
lines: Antisemitism persists across Europe, even in France.
Herzl argues that Jews need a state of their own.
The movement aims at a homeland in Palestine.

who.name: Klemens von Metternich
who.role: Austrian foreign minister and host of the congress

what.head: Putting Europe back together
lines: The great powers meet after defeating Napoleon.
They restore kings and redraw borders for a balance of power.
Europe avoids a general war for almost a century.

what.head: A thousand volunteers
lines: Sails to Sicily with a volunteer army.
Conquers the south in a few months.
Hands it to King Victor Emmanuel II to create Italy.

what.head: Germany, made by war
lines: Fights Denmark, then Austria, then France.
Each victory rallies the German states to Prussia.
The German Empire is proclaimed at Versailles in 1871.

when.fine: First in Britain, then the world

who.name: Richard Arkwright
who.role: Built the first water-powered cotton mills

what.head: Machines replace hands
